posts.title: The first plum of autumn
posts.excerpt: Why the autumn card opens with a plum we put down in June.
posts.content:
In June we fill six jars with green plums, rock sugar and a young spirit. By October the plums have given everything; the wine is amber and a little smoky.

Ume, slowly is that wine with aged rum and a pinch of smoked salt. When the jars are empty, the drink leaves the card until next year.

posts.title: Cutting ice in the afternoon
posts.excerpt: One block, two hours, and why a highball needs a single spear.
posts.content:
The block arrives at two. It rests for an hour so it will not crack, then Tomo cuts it into spears for highballs and spheres for the old fashioned.

One large piece melts slowly and keeps a highball cold and sharp to the last sip. Small cubes would drown it in ten minutes.

posts.title: A tea that tastes of smoke
posts.excerpt: Roasted green tea, rye and a spoon of black sugar.
posts.content:
Roasted green tea is gentle, low in caffeine and smells of autumn bonfires. We rest rye on the leaves for a day, then stir it with a little black sugar syrup.

Without the rye it is one of our favourite drinks without spirit: the same tea, cold, with tonic and a sprig of shiso.

posts.title: The curtain and the lantern
posts.excerpt: There is no sign on Kiri Alley. Here is how to find the door.
posts.content:
From the west exit, walk five minutes towards the river and turn left under the paper lantern. The alley is narrow; the curtain is linen, the colour of weak tea.

When the lantern is lit, a seat is free. When it is dark, the room is full; write to us for another evening.

posts.title: Stirred, not shaken
posts.excerpt: Why most drinks at Kasumi are stirred for forty turns.
posts.content:
Shaking adds air and cloud; stirring keeps a drink clear and silky. Spirit-only drinks, such as a martini or a Manhattan, are always stirred here.

Forty turns over large ice is usually right. Sayo listens for the moment the spoon stops ringing.

posts.title: A highball for the end of summer
posts.excerpt: Pressed pear, cold soda and a quiet blended whisky.
posts.content:
The last week of summer brings the first pears. We press them each evening, so the juice is never more than a few hours old.

The pear highball is the simplest drink on the card and the one most guests order twice.
